content: Pelvic girdle pain (PGP) is a distinct type of low back pain that can occur independently or alongside low back pain. It is commonly associated with pregnancy, trauma, or reactive arthritis. The pain is localized between the posterior iliac crest and the gluteal fold, particularly near the sacroiliac joints, and may radiate to the posterior thigh. It can also occur in the symphysis, either in combination with or separate from other areas. PGP often reduces the ability to stand, walk, or sit for extended periods. Diagnosis is made after ruling out lumbar spine causes, and the pain or functional impairments must be reproducible through specific clinical tests. The posterior pelvic pain provocation test and the active straight leg raise test are the most studied diagnostic tools for PGP, demonstrating acceptable reliability and validity. Approximately 20% of pregnant women experience PGP, and while most recover postpartum, some women continue to suffer from pain and disability, significantly impacting their quality of life. Women with PGP often report greater disability compared to those with low back pain, particularly when all three pelvic joints (the symphysis and both sacroiliac joints) are involved. The exact causes of PGP remain unclear but are likely multifactorial, involving hormonal changes, biomechanical stress, ligament strain, and impaired motor control. The role of the hormone relaxin in PGP is inconclusive due to conflicting evidence. Studies have shown minimal movement in the sacroiliac joints, but increased motion in the symphysis during pregnancy and postpartum in women with PGP. The pelvis plays a critical role in transferring load from the trunk to the legs, requiring optimal stability through form closure (anatomical ridges and grooves) and force closure (muscle, fascia, and ligament compression). Dysfunction in these mechanisms, such as asymmetric sacroiliac joint laxity, has been linked to moderate to severe PGP symptoms. Ligament overload, particularly in the sacrospinous and long dorsal sacroiliac ligaments, is a potential source of pain in PGP. Pain in these ligaments can disrupt muscle activity, leading to excessive stabilization, a pattern observed in PGP patients. Pregnancy-related changes in spinal curvature, such as increased lumbar lordosis or kyphosis, may also contribute to PGP by altering pelvic ligament stress. Evidence suggests that PGP is associated with altered pelvic mechanics and motor control, including dysfunction in the lumbopelvic stabilizing muscles, such as the transverse abdominals and pelvic floor muscles. Women with PGP have shown reduced trunk muscle endurance and hip extension strength, supporting the hypothesis of muscle dysfunction. Persistent PGP may result from abnormal motor control patterns, which can impair walking and other activities. Improvements in motor control have been linked to reduced pain and disability, but limited understanding of PGP mechanisms hinders effective treatment. Physical therapy interventions for PGP include exercise therapy, physical conditioning, manual therapy, pelvic belts, massage, and electrotherapy. Education is often provided alongside these treatments. Exercise therapy involves supervised or prescribed activities to improve muscle strength, flexibility, motor control, and cardiovascular fitness. Individualized exercise programs can prevent pain during weight-bearing activities. Physical conditioning, often part of return-to-work strategies, includes structured tasks and exercises to improve physical and psychological tolerance. Manual therapy, such as joint mobilization and manipulation, aims to restore normal joint motion and reduce mechanical stress. Pelvic belts, used for centuries, provide support and stability to the pelvis. They may reduce ligament strain and sacroiliac joint motion, particularly in the sagittal plane. Massage therapy, which involves soft tissue manipulation, can promote relaxation, reduce pain, and stimulate the release of endorphins and serotonin. Therapeutic ultrasound delivers high-frequency sound waves to tissues, potentially reducing pain and promoting healing, though its clinical significance remains uncertain. Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) uses electrical currents to block pain signals and reduce pain perception. Patient education programs aim to empower individuals to manage their PGP, reduce anxiety about serious outcomes, and encourage a return to normal activities. PGP significantly impacts daily life, including walking, lifting, climbing stairs, and even personal relationships. Women with PGP report lower health-related quality of life compared to healthy individuals, with physical limitations being a major contributing factor. Persistent PGP after childbirth can impair participation in both paid and unpaid work, posing challenges for individuals and society. Limited knowledge among healthcare providers about effective treatments further complicates management. A comprehensive review of physical therapy interventions for postpartum PGP is essential to guide evidence-based care.
